title: 13. Scaling to Millions: Handling Millions of Concurrent Requests — Deep Dive
summary: Covers What Actually Happens When 1 Million Users Hit Your System at the Same Time, The Core Problem, RAG at Scale, Three Golden Rules, File Upload Pipeline and more.
objectives: What Actually Happens When 1 Million Users Hit Your System at the Same Time

sections.title: 1. The Core Problem
sections.body:
### What Happens When 1M Users Hit Your Server?

```
YOU have 1 FastAPI server.
1,000,000 users upload a document AT THE SAME TIME.

Here's what happens second by second:

Second 1:
  → 50,000 HTTP connections arrive
  → Your server accepts ~1000 (FastAPI limit with Uvicorn)
  → 49,000 connections QUEUED at Nginx/OS level
  → OS TCP queue fills up → connections start DROPPING

Second 2:
  → First 1000 requests try to:
    1. Read file from request body → RAM fills up (each PDF = 5MB → 5GB RAM for 1000!)
    2. Save file to disk → Disk I/O saturated
    3. Parse PDF → CPU maxed (PDF parsing is CPU-heavy)
    4. Create chunks → More CPU
    5. Call OpenAI embedding API → Rate limited (3,500 RPM on basic tier)
    6. Write to PostgreSQL/pgvector → Connection pool exhausted

Second 3:
  → Server RAM: 32GB → OUT OF MEMORY 💀
  → CPU: 100% → UNRESPONSIVE
  → Database: max_connections reached → CONNECTION REFUSED
  → OpenAI API: Rate limited → 429 TOO MANY REQUESTS
  → Your server is DEAD. 999,000 users see errors.

THIS is why you need the patterns in this module.
```

### The Fundamental Truth

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                                                                  ║
║   You CANNOT process 1 million requests simultaneously.          ║
║                                                                  ║
║   Instead, you ACCEPT them fast, QUEUE them, and                 ║
║   PROCESS them as fast as your resources allow.                  ║
║                                                                  ║
║   The user doesn't need instant processing.                      ║
║   The user needs instant ACKNOWLEDGMENT.                         ║
║                                                                  ║
║   "Your document is being processed" ← 50ms response            ║
║   vs                                                             ║
║   Waiting 30 seconds and getting a timeout ← Dead server         ║
║                                                                  ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

diagrams.title: Keep the request path fast — push heavy work to workers
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  u["Upload / heavy request"] --> api["API: validate, store, enqueue"]
  api -->|"202 Accepted + job id"| u
  api --> q[["Queue"]]
  q --> w1["Worker pool: parse, embed, transcode"]
  w1 --> st[("Results store")]
  u -.->|"poll / SSE for status"| api
  w1 -.->|"autoscale on queue depth"| q
diagrams.explain: The rule behind handling millions of requests: never do slow work inside the request. The API validates, stores the input, enqueues a job and returns **202** with a job id in milliseconds. A worker pool, scaled on queue depth, does the heavy lifting (parsing, embedding, transcoding), and the client follows progress by polling or SSE.

sections.title: 2. RAG at Scale
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- ❌ THE WRONG WAY — Synchronous processing in the request handler
- This handles ~10 users. At 100 users your server is dead.
- Step 1: Read entire file into memory (5MB × 1000 users = 5GB RAM!)
- Step 2: Save to local disk (what if you have 4 servers? file is on only 1!)
- Step 3: Parse PDF (CPU-heavy — blocks the event loop for 5-30 seconds!)
- Step 4: Chunk (fast, but still blocking)
- Step 5: Generate embeddings (calls OpenAI API — rate limited!)
- If you have 1000 chunks and OpenAI allows 3500 RPM...

### The RAG Pipeline — What Needs to Scale

```
User uploads document → Your system must:

Step 1: ACCEPT upload           (I/O bound — network, disk)
Step 2: STORE file              (I/O bound — S3/disk)
Step 3: PARSE document          (CPU bound — PDF/DOCX parsing)
Step 4: CHUNK text              (CPU bound — text splitting)
Step 5: GENERATE embeddings     (API bound — OpenAI/Cohere rate limits)
Step 6: STORE in vector DB      (I/O bound — database writes)
Step 7: CONFIRM to user         (I/O bound — response)

Each step has a DIFFERENT bottleneck. You solve each differently.
```

### The Wrong Way (What Most Tutorials Teach)

```python
# ❌ THE WRONG WAY — Synchronous processing in the request handler
# This handles ~10 users. At 100 users your server is dead.

@app.post("/documents/upload")
async def upload_document(file: UploadFile, user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    # Step 1: Read entire file into memory (5MB × 1000 users = 5GB RAM!)
    content = await file.read()

    # Step 2: Save to local disk (what if you have 4 servers? file is on only 1!)
    file_path = f"./uploads/{file.filename}"
    with open(file_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(content)

    # Step 3: Parse PDF (CPU-heavy — blocks the event loop for 5-30 seconds!)
    loader = PyPDFLoader(file_path)
    documents = loader.load()  # ← Blocks EVERYTHING for 5-30 seconds

    # Step 4: Chunk (fast, but still blocking)
    splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000)
    chunks = splitter.split_documents(documents)

    # Step 5: Generate embeddings (calls OpenAI API — rate limited!)
    # If you have 1000 chunks and OpenAI allows 3500 RPM...
    embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings()
    vector_store = PGVector.from_documents(chunks, embeddings)  # ← 30-60 seconds!

    # Total time: 30-120 seconds PER REQUEST
    # User waited 2 minutes. 999 other users got TIMEOUT errors.
    return {"status": "done", "chunks": len(chunks)}
```

### The Right Way (Production Architecture for Millions)

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     API Layer (FastAPI)                               │
│  - Accept upload                                                     │
│  - Stream file to S3 (NOT to memory or local disk)                  │
│  - Create job record in database (status: "queued")                  │
│  - Push job to message queue                                         │
│  - Return job_id to user immediately (50ms response!)                │
└─────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │ (message queue)
                          ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Worker Pool (Celery / Custom Workers)                 │
│                                                                      │
│  Worker 1 ─┐                                                        │
│  Worker 2 ─┤  Each worker:                                          │
│  Worker 3 ─┤  1. Download file from S3                              │
│  Worker 4 ─┤  2. Parse document                                     │
│  Worker 5 ─┤  3. Split into chunks                                  │
│  ...       ─┤  4. Batch embed (500 chunks at once, not 1 by 1)      │
│  Worker 50 ─┘  5. Store in vector DB                                │
│                 6. Update status to "completed"                      │
│                                                                      │
│  Auto-scales: 5 workers normally → 50 workers during peak           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               User Checks Progress                                   │
│  GET /documents/{job_id}/status                                      │
│  → {"status": "processing", "progress": 65}                         │
│  → {"status": "completed", "chunks": 342}                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.title: 3. Three Golden Rules
sections.body:
```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                                                                      ║
║  RULE 1: NEVER do heavy work inside the request handler              ║
║          Accept fast → Queue → Process in background                 ║
║                                                                      ║
║  RULE 2: NEVER store files on the app server                         ║
║          Use S3/Azure Blob/MinIO → Any worker can access the file    ║
║                                                                      ║
║  RULE 3: NEVER process one item at a time                            ║
║          Batch everything — batch embeddings, batch DB writes        ║
║                                                                      ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

sections.title: 4. File Upload Pipeline
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- This endpoint handles 10,000+ uploads/second because: 1.
- User polls this to check progress
- Generate a presigned URL.
- Called after client uploads to S3
- ✅ THE RIGHT WAY — Stream directly to S3, never hold in memory
- Generate unique ID for this job
- Validate file BEFORE uploading
- Stream file to S3 — NEVER loads entire file into memory

**Defines:** `upload_document()`, `check_status()`, `get_upload_url()`, `start_processing()`

### Step 1: Accept Upload Without Dying

```python
# ✅ THE RIGHT WAY — Stream directly to S3, never hold in memory

import boto3
from fastapi import UploadFile, BackgroundTasks
from uuid import uuid4

s3_client = boto3.client("s3")
BUCKET = "my-rag-documents"

@app.post("/documents/upload")
async def upload_document(
    file: UploadFile,
    user: User = Depends(get_current_user)
):
    """
    This endpoint handles 10,000+ uploads/second because:
    1. File streams to S3 (NOT loaded into memory)
    2. Heavy processing goes to queue
    3. Returns immediately with a job_id
    """
    # Generate unique ID for this job
    job_id = str(uuid4())

    # Validate file BEFORE uploading
    if file.size > 50 * 1024 * 1024:  # 50MB max
        raise HTTPException(413, "File too large. Maximum 50MB.")

    allowed_types = [".pdf", ".docx", ".txt", ".csv", ".md"]
    ext = Path(file.filename).suffix.lower()
    if ext not in allowed_types:
        raise HTTPException(400, f"Unsupported file type: {ext}")

    # Stream file to S3 — NEVER loads entire file into memory
    s3_key = f"uploads/{user.id}/{job_id}/{file.filename}"

    s3_client.upload_fileobj(
        file.file,          # Stream — reads in chunks automatically
        BUCKET,
        s3_key,
        ExtraArgs={
            "ContentType": file.content_type,
            "Metadata": {"user_id": str(user.id), "job_id": job_id}
        }
    )

    # Create job record in database
    await db.execute(
        insert(ProcessingJob).values(
            id=job_id,
            user_id=user.id,
            filename=file.filename,
            s3_key=s3_key,
            file_size=file.size,
            status="queued",       # Not "processing" — it's in the queue
            created_at=datetime.utcnow()
        )
    )

    # Push to message queue (Celery/RabbitMQ/Redis)
    celery_app.send_task(
        "process_document",
        args=[job_id, user.id, s3_key, file.filename],
        queue="document_processing",      # Dedicated queue for doc processing
        priority=get_user_priority(user)  # Pro users get higher priority
    )

    # Return IMMEDIATELY — user doesn't wait for processing
    return {
        "job_id": job_id,
        "status": "queued",
        "message": "Document uploaded. Processing will begin shortly.",
        "check_status_url": f"/documents/{job_id}/status"
    }
    # Total response time: ~200ms (upload to S3 + DB insert + queue push)

@app.get("/documents/{job_id}/status")
async def check_status(job_id: str, user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    """User polls this to check progress"""
    job = await db.get(ProcessingJob, job_id)

    if not job or job.user_id != user.id:
        raise HTTPException(404, "Job not found")

    return {
        "job_id": job_id,
        "status": job.status,       # queued → processing → chunking → embedding → completed
        "progress": job.progress,   # 0 - 100
        "total_chunks": job.total_chunks,
        "error": job.error_message,
        "created_at": job.created_at,
        "completed_at": job.completed_at
    }
```

### Why Stream to S3 Instead of Local Disk?

```
Local disk storage (❌ WRONG):
  ┌──────────┐
  │ Server 1 │ ← File saved here
  │ /uploads │
  └──────────┘
  ┌──────────┐
  │ Server 2 │ ← Worker here CANNOT access the file!
  └──────────┘
  ┌──────────┐
  │ Server 3 │ ← Worker here CANNOT access the file!
  └──────────┘

S3/Object storage (✅ RIGHT):
  ┌──────────┐
  │ Server 1 │ ─upload─→ ┌────────┐
  └──────────┘            │   S3   │ ← Any server/worker can download
  ┌──────────┐            │ Bucket │
  │ Worker 1 │ ─download→ │        │
  └──────────┘            │        │
  ┌──────────┐            │        │
  │ Worker 5 │ ─download→ │        │
  └──────────┘            └────────┘

  S3 handles: ∞ concurrent reads/writes, 99.999999999% durability
  Your disk handles: maybe 1000 IOPS before it's saturated
```

### Presigned Upload URL (Even Better — Client Uploads Directly to S3)

```python
# ✅ BEST — Client uploads directly to S3. Your server never touches the file!

@app.post("/documents/get-upload-url")
async def get_upload_url(
    filename: str,
    content_type: str,
    user: User = Depends(get_current_user)
):
    """
    Generate a presigned URL. Client uploads DIRECTLY to S3.
    Your server handles ZERO file bytes → can handle unlimited uploads!
    """
    job_id = str(uuid4())
    s3_key = f"uploads/{user.id}/{job_id}/{filename}"

    # Generate presigned URL (valid for 15 min)
    presigned_url = s3_client.generate_presigned_url(
        "put_object",
        Params={
            "Bucket": BUCKET,
            "Key": s3_key,
            "ContentType": content_type
        },
        ExpiresIn=900  # 15 minutes
    )

    # Create job record (pending upload)
    await db.execute(
        insert(ProcessingJob).values(
            id=job_id, user_id=user.id, filename=filename,
            s3_key=s3_key, status="awaiting_upload"
        )
    )

    return {
        "upload_url": presigned_url,  # Client POSTs file here
        "job_id": job_id,
        "expires_in": 900
    }

# Client-side (JavaScript):
# const { upload_url, job_id } = await api.post("/documents/get-upload-url", {...})
# await fetch(upload_url, { method: "PUT", body: file })
# await api.post(`/documents/${job_id}/start-processing`)

@app.post("/documents/{job_id}/start-processing")
async def start_processing(job_id: str, user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    """Called after client uploads to S3"""
    job = await db.get(ProcessingJob, job_id)

    # Verify file exists in S3
    s3_client.head_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key=job.s3_key)

    # Queue for processing
    celery_app.send_task("process_document", args=[job_id])

    return {"status": "queued", "job_id": job_id}
```

```
Flow comparison:

Traditional upload (server handles file bytes):
  Client → [5MB file] → Server → [5MB file] → S3
  Server memory used: 5MB per concurrent upload
  1000 concurrent uploads = 5GB RAM just for file holding!

Presigned URL (server handles ZERO file bytes):
  Client --(get URL)-→ Server (returns URL, 1KB response)
  Client → [5MB file] → S3 directly
  Server memory used: 0 bytes!
  1,000,000 concurrent uploads = server just returns URLs!
```

sections.title: 5. Document Processing at Scale
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- This runs in a WORKER PROCESS, not in the API server.
- Step 1: Download from S3 to temp file
- Step 2: Parse document
- Step 3: Split into chunks
- Add metadata to every chunk
- Step 4: Generate embeddings IN BATCHES (critical for scale!)
- See Section 6 below for the batching code
- Retry with exponential backoff

### The Worker That Processes Documents

```python
# workers/document_worker.py
import boto3, tempfile, os
from celery import Celery
from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader, Docx2txtLoader, TextLoader
from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

celery_app = Celery("workers", broker="redis://redis:6379/0")
s3 = boto3.client("s3")

@celery_app.task(
    bind=True,
    name="process_document",
    max_retries=3,
    default_retry_delay=60,
    acks_late=True,             # Don't acknowledge until complete (crash safety)
    reject_on_worker_lost=True  # Re-queue if worker crashes mid-processing
)
def process_document(self, job_id: str, user_id: int, s3_key: str, filename: str):
    """
    This runs in a WORKER PROCESS, not in the API server.
    Even if 1 million documents are queued, workers process
    them one at a time (per worker). 50 workers = 50 documents
    processing simultaneously.
    """
    try:
        # Update status
        update_job_status(job_id, "processing", progress=0)

        # Step 1: Download from S3 to temp file
        with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=os.path.splitext(filename)[1], delete=False) as tmp:
            s3.download_fileobj("my-rag-documents", s3_key, tmp)
            tmp_path = tmp.name

        update_job_status(job_id, "processing", progress=10)

        # Step 2: Parse document
        if filename.endswith(".pdf"):
            loader = PyPDFLoader(tmp_path)
        elif filename.endswith(".docx"):
            loader = Docx2txtLoader(tmp_path)
        else:
            loader = TextLoader(tmp_path)

        raw_docs = loader.load()
        update_job_status(job_id, "parsing_complete", progress=30)

        # Step 3: Split into chunks
        splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
            chunk_size=1000,
            chunk_overlap=200,
            separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""]
        )
        chunks = splitter.split_documents(raw_docs)

        # Add metadata to every chunk
        for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
            chunk.metadata.update({
                "user_id": str(user_id),
                "job_id": job_id,
                "source_file": filename,
                "chunk_index": i,
                "total_chunks": len(chunks)
            })

        update_job_status(job_id, "chunking_complete", progress=50,
                          extra={"total_chunks": len(chunks)})

        # Step 4: Generate embeddings IN BATCHES (critical for scale!)
        # See Section 6 below for the batching code
        batch_embed_and_store(chunks, user_id, job_id)

        update_job_status(job_id, "completed", progress=100)

        # Cleanup temp file
        os.unlink(tmp_path)

    except Exception as exc:
        update_job_status(job_id, "failed", error=str(exc))
        # Retry with exponential backoff
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=60 * (2 ** self.request.retries))
```

### Scaling Workers with Celery

```python
# celery_config.py

celery_app = Celery("workers")

celery_app.conf.update(
    broker_url="redis://redis:6379/0",
    result_backend="redis://redis:6379/1",

    # Worker configuration
    worker_concurrency=4,          # 4 tasks per worker process
    worker_prefetch_multiplier=2,  # Pre-fetch 2 tasks
    worker_max_tasks_per_child=100,  # Restart worker after 100 tasks (prevent memory leaks)

    # Queue routing — different queues for different task types
    task_routes={
        "process_document": {"queue": "document_processing"},
        "generate_embeddings": {"queue": "embedding"},
        "send_notification": {"queue": "notifications"},
    },

    # Rate limiting per task type
    task_annotations={
        "generate_embeddings": {
            "rate_limit": "100/m"  # Max 100 embedding tasks per minute (OpenAI limits)
        }
    },

    # Priority queues (Pro users processed first)
    broker_transport_options={
        "priority_steps": list(range(10)),  # 0 (highest) to 9 (lowest)
    }
)
```

```bash
# Start workers

# 10 document processing workers (CPU-heavy tasks)
celery -A celery_config worker \
    --queue=document_processing \
    --concurrency=4 \
    --loglevel=info \
    --hostname=doc-worker-%h

# 5 embedding workers (API-bound tasks)
celery -A celery_config worker \
    --queue=embedding \
    --concurrency=10 \
    --loglevel=info \
    --hostname=embed-worker-%h

# 3 notification workers (lightweight tasks)
celery -A celery_config worker \
    --queue=notifications \
    --concurrency=20 \
    --loglevel=info \
    --hostname=notif-worker-%h

# Auto-scale workers based on queue depth
celery -A celery_config worker \
    --queue=document_processing \
    --autoscale=20,4 \  # Scale between 4 and 20 concurrent tasks
    --loglevel=info
```

### How 1 Million Documents Get Processed

```
Time 0:00 — 1,000,000 documents uploaded
  → API accepts all uploads in ~10 minutes (1,700 uploads/sec)
  → All files are in S3
  → All jobs are in the queue

Queue state: 1,000,000 jobs waiting
Workers: 50 workers × 4 concurrency = 200 documents processing simultaneously

Time 0:10 — Workers start processing
  → 200 documents processed per batch
  → Average processing time per document: 30 seconds
  → Throughput: 200 / 30 × 60 = 400 documents per minute

  Wait... 1,000,000 / 400 = 2,500 minutes = 41 hours?!

  SOLUTION: Auto-scale workers!

Time 0:15 — Auto-scaler detects queue depth > 10,000
  → Scales from 50 workers to 500 workers
  → 500 × 4 = 2,000 concurrent
  → Throughput: ~4,000 documents per minute

  1,000,000 / 4,000 = 250 minutes ≈ 4 hours

Time 0:30 — Auto-scaler scales to 2,000 workers
  → 8,000 concurrent
  → BUT: OpenAI embedding API rate limit is the bottleneck now!
  → Switch to self-hosted embedding model (see Section 6)

Time 1:00 — With self-hosted embeddings + 2,000 workers
  → ~15,000 documents per minute
  → 1,000,000 / 15,000 ≈ 67 minutes!

TIMELINE:
  ├── 0:00  All uploads accepted (users get job_id)
  ├── 0:10  Workers start processing
  ├── 0:30  Auto-scaled to 2,000 workers
  ├── 0:45  500,000 documents processed
  ├── 1:07  All 1,000,000 documents processed ✅

  Users see: "Processing" → "Complete" (within 1-60 min depending on queue position)
  No user saw an ERROR. No server crashed.
```

sections.title: 6. Embedding at Scale
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Embed thousands of chunks efficiently using batching.
- Process chunks: batch embed and batch insert
- Insert thousands of vectors in one database transaction
- INSERT INTO document_embeddings (content, embedding, source_file, user_id, chunk_index) VALUES %s
- Step 1: Batch embed
- Step 2: Batch insert into vector DB (NOT one at a time!)
- ❌ SLOW: One insert per vector
- For i in range(len(texts)):

**Defines:** `batch_embed()`, `batch_embed_and_store()`, `batch_insert_vectors()`, `local_batch_embed()`, `embed()`

### The Embedding Bottleneck

```
The Problem:
  1 document = ~50 chunks
  1,000,000 documents = 50,000,000 chunks to embed!

  OpenAI Embedding API:
    - Rate limit: 3,500 requests/minute (basic tier)
    - Each request can embed up to 2048 tokens
    - If you send 1 chunk per request: 50M / 3,500 = 14,286 minutes = 10 DAYS!

  BUT: OpenAI allows BATCH embedding (multiple chunks per request)!
    - Batch size: up to 2048 inputs per request
    - 50M / 2048 = 24,414 requests
    - 24,414 / 3,500 per min = 7 minutes!
    - (In practice, limited by token count, so ~30-60 minutes)
```

### Batch Embedding Implementation

```python
# services/embedding_service.py

from openai import AsyncOpenAI
import asyncio
from typing import List

client = AsyncOpenAI()

async def batch_embed(texts: List[str], batch_size: int = 500) -> List[List[float]]:
    """
    Embed thousands of chunks efficiently using batching.

    Instead of: 1 API call per chunk (N calls)
    We do:      1 API call per 500 chunks (N/500 calls = 99.8% fewer API calls!)
    """
    all_embeddings = []

    for i in range(0, len(texts), batch_size):
        batch = texts[i:i + batch_size]

        response = await client.embeddings.create(
            model="text-embedding-3-small",
            input=batch  # Send 500 texts at once!
        )

        batch_embeddings = [item.embedding for item in response.data]
        all_embeddings.extend(batch_embeddings)

        # Respect rate limits
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)  # Small delay between batches

    return all_embeddings

def batch_embed_and_store(chunks, user_id: int, job_id: str):
    """Process chunks: batch embed and batch insert"""

    texts = [chunk.page_content for chunk in chunks]
    metadatas = [chunk.metadata for chunk in chunks]

    # Step 1: Batch embed
    embeddings = asyncio.run(batch_embed(texts, batch_size=500))

    # Step 2: Batch insert into vector DB (NOT one at a time!)
    batch_insert_vectors(texts, embeddings, metadatas, user_id)

def batch_insert_vectors(texts, embeddings, metadatas, user_id: int):
    """Insert thousands of vectors in one database transaction"""

    # ❌ SLOW: One insert per vector
    # for i in range(len(texts)):
    #     db.execute("INSERT INTO embeddings ...")  # 50,000 round trips!

    # ✅ FAST: Batch insert (all vectors in one transaction)
    import psycopg2

    conn = psycopg2.connect(DATABASE_URL)
    cur = conn.cursor()

    # Use COPY or execute_values for bulk insert
    from psycopg2.extras import execute_values

    values = [
        (texts[i], embeddings[i], metadatas[i]["source_file"],
         str(user_id), metadatas[i]["chunk_index"])
        for i in range(len(texts))
    ]

    execute_values(
        cur,
        """
        INSERT INTO document_embeddings
        (content, embedding, source_file, user_id, chunk_index)
        VALUES %s
        """,
        values,
        page_size=1000  # Insert 1000 rows at a time
    )
    conn.commit()

    # 50,000 vectors inserted in ~2 seconds instead of 50,000 round trips!
```

### Self-Hosted Embeddings (No Rate Limits, 10x Cheaper)

```python
# When OpenAI rate limits are the bottleneck, host your own embedding model

# Option 1: sentence-transformers (runs on your GPU server)
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")  # 384 dimensions, very fast

def local_batch_embed(texts: list[str], batch_size: int = 256) -> list:
    """
    Self-hosted embeddings:
    - No rate limits
    - No API costs
    - ~10,000 embeddings/second on a single GPU
    - ~1,000 embeddings/second on CPU

    50,000,000 chunks / 10,000 per second = 83 minutes on 1 GPU
    With 10 GPU workers: ~8 minutes!
    """
    all_embeddings = []
    for i in range(0, len(texts), batch_size):
        batch = texts[i:i + batch_size]
        embeddings = model.encode(batch, show_progress_bar=False)
        all_embeddings.extend(embeddings.tolist())
    return all_embeddings

# Option 2: FastAPI embedding microservice (deploy separately, scale independently)
# embedding_service/main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

app = FastAPI()
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

@app.post("/embed")
async def embed(texts: list[str]):
    embeddings = model.encode(texts)
    return {"embeddings": embeddings.tolist()}

# docker-compose up -d --scale embedding-service=10
```

sections.title: 7. Vector Search at Scale
sections.body:
### When 1M Users Query Their Documents Simultaneously

```
The Query Path (happens at request time — must be FAST):

User asks: "What is the refund policy?"
  1. Generate embedding for the question           → 20ms
  2. Search vector DB for similar chunks            → 5-50ms
  3. Retrieve top 5 chunks                          → 5ms
  4. Send chunks + question to LLM                  → 1-5 seconds
  5. Stream response to user                        → 2-10 seconds

Steps 1-3 take <100ms — these are fine.
Step 4-5 (LLM call) is the REAL bottleneck.
```

### Vector Database Scaling Strategies

```python
# pgvector — scaling for millions of vectors

# 1. Create optimized table
"""
CREATE TABLE document_embeddings (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    embedding vector(384) NOT NULL,  -- 384 dimensions for MiniLM
    source_file VARCHAR(500),
    metadata JSONB,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- CRITICAL: Create HNSW index for fast similarity search
-- Without index: Full scan of all vectors → O(n) → MINUTES for millions
-- With HNSW index: Approximate nearest neighbor → O(log n) → MILLISECONDS

CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_hnsw ON document_embeddings
    USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
    WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 200);

-- Partition by user_id for multi-tenant isolation AND performance
-- Each user's vectors are in their own partition → scans only their data

CREATE TABLE document_embeddings (
    id BIGSERIAL,
    user_id VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    embedding vector(384) NOT NULL,
    source_file VARCHAR(500)
) PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);

-- Create 16 partitions (can scale to 256, 1024, etc.)
CREATE TABLE embeddings_p0 PARTITION OF document_embeddings
    FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 16, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE embeddings_p1 PARTITION OF document_embeddings
    FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 16, REMAINDER 1);
-- ... up to p15

-- Each partition gets its own HNSW index
CREATE INDEX idx_embed_p0_hnsw ON embeddings_p0
    USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
"""

# 2. Query with user isolation (reads only their partition)
async def search_similar(question: str, user_id: str, k: int = 5):
    question_embedding = await embed_single(question)

    results = await db.fetch("""
        SELECT content, source_file,
               1 - (embedding <=> $1::vector) as similarity
        FROM document_embeddings
        WHERE user_id = $2
        ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector
        LIMIT $3
    """, question_embedding, user_id, k)

    return results
    # With HNSW index + partition: 5-20ms even with 100M vectors!
```

### Caching Popular Queries

```python
# Cache frequent questions — many users ask similar things

async def cached_rag_query(question: str, user_id: str):
    # 1. Check cache first
    cache_key = f"rag:{user_id}:{hashlib.md5(question.encode()).hexdigest()}"
    cached = await redis.get(cache_key)
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)  # Cache hit — instant response!

    # 2. Cache miss — do the full RAG pipeline
    chunks = await search_similar(question, user_id)
    answer = await call_llm(question, chunks)

    # 3. Cache for 1 hour
    await redis.setex(cache_key, 3600, json.dumps(answer))

    return answer
```

sections.title: 8. Millions of API Requests
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Buffer writes and flush in batches
- Runs every 30 seconds — batch update all changed like counts
- Examples: Product page, User profile, Feed, Search results
- Layer 1: Local in-memory cache (fastest, per-server)
- Layer 2: Redis cache (shared across servers)
- Layer 3: Read replica (not primary DB)
- 99% of requests → Local cache → 0.01ms
- 0.9% of requests → Redis → 1ms

**Defines:** `get_product()`, `WriteBuffer`, `like_post()`, `sync_likes_to_db()`, `resize_image()`, `charge()`, `process_payment()`

### Beyond RAG — How to Handle ANY Type of Million Concurrent Requests

```
Every scenario follows the same pattern:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                  │
│    FAST LAYER (handles millions)                                 │
│    ─────────────────────────────                                │
│    CDN → Load Balancer → API Gateway → Rate Limiter              │
│                                                                  │
│    PROCESSING LAYER (does the heavy work)                        │
│    ──────────────────────────────────────                        │
│    Message Queue → Worker Pool → Auto-Scaling                    │
│                                                                  │
│    DATA LAYER (stores results)                                   │
│    ───────────────────────────                                  │
│    Cache (Redis) → Database → Object Storage                     │
│                                                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Pattern: Read-Heavy (90% of traffic)

```python
# Examples: Product page, User profile, Feed, Search results
# Solution: Cache aggressively

@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
async def get_product(product_id: int):
    # Layer 1: Local in-memory cache (fastest, per-server)
    local = local_cache.get(f"product:{product_id}")
    if local:
        return local  # 0.01ms

    # Layer 2: Redis cache (shared across servers)
    cached = await redis.get(f"product:{product_id}")
    if cached:
        data = json.loads(cached)
        local_cache.set(f"product:{product_id}", data, ttl=60)
        return data  # 1ms

    # Layer 3: Read replica (not primary DB)
    product = await read_db.get_product(product_id)

    # Populate caches
    await redis.setex(f"product:{product_id}", 300, json.dumps(product))
    local_cache.set(f"product:{product_id}", product, ttl=60)

    return product  # 10-50ms

# Result:
#   99% of requests → Local cache → 0.01ms
#   0.9% of requests → Redis → 1ms
#   0.1% of requests → Database → 50ms
#   Average: ~0.2ms per request
#   1 server handles: 5,000,000 req/min easily!
```

### Pattern: Write-Heavy (High Throughput)

```python
# Examples: Logging, Analytics, IoT sensor data, Like/View counts
# Solution: Buffer writes, batch insert

class WriteBuffer:
    """Buffer writes and flush in batches"""

    def __init__(self, flush_size: int = 1000, flush_interval: int = 5):
        self.buffer = []
        self.flush_size = flush_size
        self.flush_interval = flush_interval

    async def add(self, record: dict):
        self.buffer.append(record)

        if len(self.buffer) >= self.flush_size:
            await self.flush()

    async def flush(self):
        if not self.buffer:
            return

        records = self.buffer.copy()
        self.buffer.clear()

        # Batch insert (1 query for 1000 records instead of 1000 queries)
        await db.execute_many(
            "INSERT INTO analytics (user_id, event, data, timestamp) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)",
            [(r["user_id"], r["event"], r["data"], r["ts"]) for r in records]
        )

# For likes/views: Use Redis atomic increment, sync to DB periodically
@app.post("/posts/{post_id}/like")
async def like_post(post_id: int, user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    # Atomic increment in Redis (handles 100K+ likes/sec)
    await redis.incr(f"post:{post_id}:likes")
    await redis.sadd(f"post:{post_id}:liked_by", user.id)
    return {"status": "liked"}

# Background task syncs to DB every 30 seconds
@celery_app.task
def sync_likes_to_db():
    """Runs every 30 seconds — batch update all changed like counts"""
    keys = redis.keys("post:*:likes")
    for key in keys:
        post_id = key.split(":")[1]
        likes = redis.get(key)
        db.execute("UPDATE posts SET likes_count = %s WHERE id = %s", [likes, post_id])
```

### Pattern: CPU-Heavy (Computation)

```python
# Examples: Image processing, Video transcoding, PDF parsing, ML inference
# Solution: ALWAYS offload to workers

# ❌ NEVER do this in a request handler
@app.post("/images/resize")
async def resize_image(file: UploadFile):
    image = Image.open(file.file)
    resized = image.resize((800, 600))  # CPU-heavy! Blocks event loop!
    # ...

# ✅ ALWAYS queue CPU-heavy work
@app.post("/images/resize")
async def resize_image(file: UploadFile):
    # Save to S3, queue for processing
    s3_key = await upload_to_s3(file)
    job_id = queue_task("resize_image", s3_key=s3_key)
    return {"job_id": job_id, "status": "processing"}
```

### Pattern: External API Dependent

```python
# Examples: Payment processing, LLM calls, Email sending, SMS
# Solution: Queue + Retry + Rate limit

# Problem: Stripe allows 100 requests/sec. You have 1000 payments/sec at peak.

# Solution: Queue payments and process at Stripe's rate
@app.post("/payments/charge")
async def charge(payment: PaymentCreate, user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    # Create pending payment record
    payment_id = await db.create_payment(payment, status="pending")

    # Queue for processing (don't call Stripe directly!)
    celery_app.send_task("process_payment", args=[payment_id])

    return {"payment_id": payment_id, "status": "processing"}

@celery_app.task(
    rate_limit="90/s",     # Process max 90/sec (under Stripe's 100/sec limit)
    max_retries=5,
    default_retry_delay=30
)
def process_payment(payment_id: str):
    try:
        payment = db.get_payment(payment_id)
        result = stripe.PaymentIntent.create(
            amount=payment.amount,
            currency="usd",
            idempotency_key=f"payment_{payment_id}"  # Prevent double charge!
        )
        db.update_payment(payment_id, status="completed", stripe_id=result.id)
    except stripe.error.RateLimitError:
        raise self.retry(countdown=10)
    except stripe.error.CardError as e:
        db.update_payment(payment_id, status="failed", error=str(e))
```

sections.title: 9. Millions of Payments
sections.body:
### Every Transaction Must: Complete, Never Duplicate, Never Lose

```python
# The Idempotency Pattern — Prevent double charges even with retries

from uuid import uuid4

@app.post("/orders/checkout")
async def checkout(
    order: OrderCreate,
    idempotency_key: str = Header(None),
    user: User = Depends(get_current_user)
):
    """
    If user clicks "Pay" twice, or network retries the request,
    the idempotency key ensures only ONE charge happens.
    """
    if not idempotency_key:
        idempotency_key = str(uuid4())

    # Check if this exact request was already processed
    existing = await redis.get(f"idempotency:{idempotency_key}")
    if existing:
        return json.loads(existing)  # Return same response as before

    # Process the order
    order_id = await create_order(order, user.id)
    result = {"order_id": order_id, "status": "created"}

    # Store result with idempotency key (24 hour TTL)
    await redis.setex(
        f"idempotency:{idempotency_key}",
        86400,
        json.dumps(result)
    )

    return result

# The Saga Pattern — Distributed transaction across services
async def process_checkout(order_id: str):
    """
    Steps that must ALL succeed, or ALL rollback:
    1. Reserve inventory
    2. Charge payment
    3. Create shipment

    If step 2 fails → Undo step 1 (release inventory)
    If step 3 fails → Undo step 2 (refund) → Undo step 1 (release)
    """
    compensations = []  # Track what to undo if something fails

    try:
        # Step 1
        await inventory_service.reserve(order_id)
        compensations.append(lambda: inventory_service.release(order_id))

        # Step 2
        await payment_service.charge(order_id)
        compensations.append(lambda: payment_service.refund(order_id))

        # Step 3
        await shipping_service.create_shipment(order_id)

        await update_order_status(order_id, "confirmed")

    except Exception as e:
        # Undo everything in reverse order
        for compensate in reversed(compensations):
            try:
                await compensate()
            except Exception:
                # Log for manual intervention
                logger.critical(f"Compensation failed for order {order_id}")

        await update_order_status(order_id, "failed")
        raise
```

sections.title: 10. Millions of Real-Time Events
sections.body:
### WebSocket Connections at Scale

```
Problem:
  1 million users connected via WebSocket for live chat.
  Each server holds 50,000 connections.
  You need 20 servers.

  User A (on Server 1) sends message to User B (on Server 15).
  Server 1 doesn't know about User B!

Solution: Redis Pub/Sub bridges all servers.

  Server 1  ──publish──→ ┌─────────────┐ ──subscribe──→ Server 15
  (User A)               │ Redis       │               (User B)
                         │ Pub/Sub     │
  Server 2 ──subscribe──→│             │──subscribe──→  Server 20
                         └─────────────┘
```

```python
# Scalable WebSocket with Redis Pub/Sub

import redis.asyncio as aioredis
from fastapi import WebSocket
import json

redis_client = aioredis.from_url("redis://redis:6379")

# In-memory connections for THIS server only
connections: dict[str, list[WebSocket]] = {}  # channel_id → [websockets]

async def websocket_handler(websocket: WebSocket, channel_id: str, user_id: str):
    await websocket.accept()

    # Track connection on this server
    if channel_id not in connections:
        connections[channel_id] = []
    connections[channel_id].append(websocket)

    # Subscribe to Redis channel (receives messages from ALL servers)
    pubsub = redis_client.pubsub()
    await pubsub.subscribe(f"chat:{channel_id}")

    try:
        # Task 1: Forward Redis messages to this WebSocket
        async def redis_listener():
            async for message in pubsub.listen():
                if message["type"] == "message":
                    await websocket.send_text(message["data"])

        # Task 2: Receive from WebSocket, publish to Redis
        async def ws_listener():
            while True:
                data = await websocket.receive_text()
                # Publish to Redis → ALL servers receive it
                await redis_client.publish(
                    f"chat:{channel_id}",
                    json.dumps({"user_id": user_id, "message": data})
                )

        await asyncio.gather(redis_listener(), ws_listener())

    finally:
        connections[channel_id].remove(websocket)
        await pubsub.unsubscribe(f"chat:{channel_id}")
```

### Server-Sent Events at Scale (For RAG streaming responses)

```python
# Streaming RAG answers to millions of users

from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

@app.post("/chat/stream")
async def stream_rag_response(
    question: str,
    user: User = Depends(get_current_user)
):
    """
    Stream RAG answer token by token.

    Even with 10,000 concurrent streaming responses:
    - Each SSE connection is lightweight (~1KB memory)
    - FastAPI async handles them concurrently
    - The LLM API is the bottleneck, not the streaming
    """
    async def generate():
        # 1. Retrieve relevant chunks (fast — 5-20ms)
        chunks = await search_similar(question, user.id)
        context = "\n".join([c["content"] for c in chunks])

        # 2. Stream from LLM
        async for token in llm.astream(
            f"Context: {context}\n\nQuestion: {question}\n\nAnswer:"
        ):
            yield f"data: {json.dumps({'token': token})}\n\n"

        # 3. Send sources at the end
        sources = [{"file": c["source_file"]} for c in chunks]
        yield f"data: {json.dumps({'sources': sources, 'done': True})}\n\n"

    return StreamingResponse(generate(), media_type="text/event-stream")
```

sections.title: 11. Millions of AI/LLM Requests
sections.body:
### The LLM is the Most Expensive Bottleneck

```
Cost and speed analysis for 1M LLM requests:

OpenAI GPT-4o:
  - $2.50 / 1M input tokens, $10 / 1M output tokens
  - Rate limit: 10,000 RPM (enterprise)
  - 1M requests / 10,000 per min = 100 minutes to process all
  - Cost: ~$5,000 (assuming 500 input + 500 output tokens each)

OpenAI GPT-4o-mini:
  - $0.15 / 1M input tokens, $0.60 / 1M output tokens
  - Rate limit: 30,000 RPM
  - 1M requests / 30,000 = 33 minutes
  - Cost: ~$375

Self-hosted (Llama 3, Mistral):
  - 10 GPU servers × $3/hour × 2 hours = $60
  - No rate limits, full control
  - Cost: ~$60 total!
```

```python
# Multi-tier LLM routing (use expensive models only when needed)

async def smart_route_llm(question: str, context: str):
    """
    Route to appropriate LLM based on complexity.
    Saves 80% of LLM costs.
    """
    # Simple questions → cheap/fast model
    if len(question) < 50 and not any(w in question.lower() for w in ["analyze", "compare", "explain"]):
        return await call_llm("gpt-4o-mini", question, context)

    # Complex questions → powerful model
    return await call_llm("gpt-4o", question, context)

# LLM request queue with rate limiting
class LLMRequestQueue:
    def __init__(self, max_concurrent: int = 100):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(max_concurrent)
        self.queue = asyncio.Queue()

    async def request(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        async with self.semaphore:  # Max 100 concurrent LLM calls
            return await call_llm_api(prompt)

llm_queue = LLMRequestQueue(max_concurrent=100)

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(question: str, user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    # All LLM calls go through the queue — prevents overwhelming the API
    chunks = await search_similar(question, user.id)
    prompt = build_prompt(question, chunks)
    answer = await llm_queue.request(prompt)
    return {"answer": answer}
```

### Semantic Cache (Don't Call LLM for Repeated Questions)

```python
# If 1000 users ask "What is the refund policy?" — call LLM ONCE

class SemanticCache:
    """Cache LLM responses by semantic similarity, not exact match"""

    def __init__(self, redis_client, similarity_threshold: float = 0.95):
        self.redis = redis_client
        self.threshold = similarity_threshold

    async def get(self, question: str, user_id: str) -> str | None:
        """Check if a similar question was already answered"""
        question_embedding = await embed_single(question)

        # Search cache vectors
        cached = await self.redis.ft("cache_idx").search(
            query=f"@user_id:{{{user_id}}}",
            vector=question_embedding,
            num_results=1
        )

        if cached and cached.similarity > self.threshold:
            return cached.answer  # 95%+ similar question already answered!

        return None

    async def set(self, question: str, answer: str, user_id: str):
        """Cache question-answer pair with embedding"""
        embedding = await embed_single(question)
        await self.redis.hset(f"cache:{hash(question)}", mapping={
            "question": question,
            "answer": answer,
            "user_id": user_id,
            "embedding": embedding,
            "created_at": time.time()
        })
        await self.redis.expire(f"cache:{hash(question)}", 3600)  # 1 hour TTL

# Usage
semantic_cache = SemanticCache(redis_client)

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(question: str, user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    # Check semantic cache first
    cached_answer = await semantic_cache.get(question, user.id)
    if cached_answer:
        return {"answer": cached_answer, "source": "cache"}  # 5ms instead of 5 seconds!

    # Cache miss — full RAG pipeline
    answer = await full_rag_pipeline(question, user.id)

    # Cache for next time
    await semantic_cache.set(question, answer, user.id)

    return {"answer": answer, "source": "live"}
```

```
│  │ 3 Read       │  │ (100M vectors)│  │ (Cache, │  │ (Unlimited)  │ │
│  │ Replicas     │  │               │  │  Queue, │  │              │ │
│  │              │  │               │  │  PubSub)│  │              │ │
│  └──────────────┘  └───────────────┘  └─────────┘  └──────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Decision Table: How to Handle Each Type of Request

```
┌────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Request Type           │ How to Handle at Scale                      │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ File Upload            │ Presigned URL → S3 direct → Queue process  │
│                        │ User gets job_id, polls for status          │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Document Processing    │ Worker pool (Celery), auto-scale workers   │
│ (PDF parse, chunk)     │ CPU-heavy → dedicated queue + workers      │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Embedding Generation   │ Batch (500 at once), self-hosted for scale │
│                        │ API-bound → rate limit + retry              │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Vector Search          │ HNSW index + partition by user              │
│                        │ Cache frequent queries in Redis             │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LLM / Chat             │ SSE streaming, semantic cache, multi-tier  │
│                        │ Queue if overloaded, priority by plan       │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Read API (GET)         │ Multi-layer cache: local → Redis → replica │
│                        │ CDN for public data                        │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Write API (POST)       │ Buffer writes, batch insert                │
│                        │ Event-driven: write → publish event         │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Payment                │ Queue + idempotency key + saga pattern     │
│                        │ Rate limit to match provider limits         │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Real-Time (WebSocket)  │ Redis Pub/Sub bridges servers              │
│                        │ 50K connections per server, scale servers   │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Email / Notification   │ Always queue, never send in request handler│
│                        │ Batch where possible                       │
├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Image / Video          │ Upload to S3 → Queue → Workers             │
│                        │ CDN for delivery                           │
└────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### The Universal Formula

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                                                                      ║
║   For ANY scenario with millions of users:                           ║
║                                                                      ║
║   1. ACCEPT the request fast (validate, save reference, return ID)  ║
║   2. QUEUE the heavy work (never block the request)                  ║
║   3. PROCESS with workers (scale workers up/down with demand)        ║
║   4. CACHE the results (avoid recomputing for similar requests)      ║
║   5. NOTIFY the user (poll endpoint, WebSocket, or email)           ║
║                                                                      ║
║   The API layer handles MILLIONS of requests per second              ║
║   because it does almost NO work — just validation + queuing.        ║
║                                                                      ║
║   The worker layer does the HEAVY work at its own pace,              ║
║   scaling up and down based on queue depth.                          ║
║                                                                      ║
║   The cache layer prevents REPEATED work — same question =           ║
║   same answer without recomputing.                                   ║
║                                                                      ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.body:
```
FOR RAG/FILE PROCESSING:
1. Upload files to S3 (presigned URL = server handles ZERO bytes)
2. Queue document processing (Celery workers, auto-scale)
3. Batch embeddings (500 chunks per API call, or self-host)
4. Batch DB inserts (execute_values, not one by one)
5. HNSW index on vector DB (O(log n) instead of O(n))
6. Semantic cache for repeated questions
7. Stream LLM responses with SSE

FOR ANY MILLION-USER SCENARIO:
1. Return fast, process later (queue everything heavy)
2. Scale horizontally (stateless servers + load balancer)
3. Cache aggressively (local → Redis → DB)
4. Batch everything (writes, embeddings, API calls)
5. Rate limit per user/IP/tier (token bucket algorithm)
6. Auto-scale workers based on queue depth
7. Use the right database for the right job (SQL, NoSQL, Vector, Cache)
8. Monitor everything (know when you're approaching limits)
```
